issue_context.title: Extra warnings
issue_context.body:
Hi,

I've rebuilt micropython for an eCos-embedded platform, based on an old plain ARM7-TDMI (ARMv4T) SoC. We usually build all our code with many extra warnings enabled, but I had to disable many of them with micropython as they kept rising. Some warnings are harmless, but some others are likely to report real potential issues.

Here is the list of warnings that I had to shut off to build micropython:
- [ ] -Wbad-function-cast
- [x] -Wdouble-promotion
- [ ] -Wfloat-equal
- [x] -Wformat
- [x] -Wmissing-declarations
- [ ] -Wmissing-format-attribute
- [x] -Wmissing-prototypes
- [x] -Wold-style-definition
- [x] -Wpointer-arith
- [x] -Wredundant-decls
- [x] -Wshadow 
- [x] -Wsign-compare
- [x] -Wstrict-prototypes
- [ ] -Wswitch-default
- [ ] -Wswitch-enum
- [x] -Wuninitialized
- [ ] -Wunsuffixed-float-constants
- [x] -Wunused-parameter

I known that I'd better come with patches, for now I've just started playing with micropython.
It may be worth adding some/all of them to the default warning list?

Compiler: arm-eabi GCC 4.9.0 / binutils 2.24

EDIT by @dpgeorge: made warnings above checkboxes.  Once checked off, core uPy passes that warning.
comments:
Related discussions are in #50 and #683.

Since uPy aims to be embedded (within some other build system), it's good to aim for it to compile with as many warnings enabled as possible.  But some will be difficult to conform to because of tricks like computed goto in the VM.

For things like suffixing a float constant, is that really necessary?
> For things like suffixing a float constant, is that really necessary?

I guess it depends on how "type" sensitive you want to be.
0.0 is a double.
0.0F is a float.

So part of suffixing properly serves as a form of documentation.

I think that since MicroPython (for stmhal) is being built with -fsingle-precision-constant it's a wash. If you ever did support a platform where you mixed floats and doubles (i.e. -fsingle-precision-constant wasn't being used) then there will definitely be differences in code generation.

I took this C file:

``` C
float func1(float a) {
    return a * 123.4;
}

float func2(float a) {
    return a * 123.4F;
}
```

and compiled it using the same command line used for the rest of stmhal, and dropped and -fsingle-precision-constant and -Wdouble-promotion) and the assembly produced looks like:

```
00000000 <func1>:
   0:   b508        push    {r3, lr}
   2:   ee10 0a10   vmov    r0, s0
   6:   f7ff fffe   bl  0 <__aeabi_f2d>
   a:   a305        add r3, pc, #20 ; (adr r3, 20 <func1+0x20>)
   c:   e9d3 2300   ldrd    r2, r3, [r3]
  10:   f7ff fffe   bl  0 <__aeabi_dmul>
  14:   f7ff fffe   bl  0 <__aeabi_d2f>
  18:   ee00 0a10   vmov    s0, r0
  1c:   bd08        pop {r3, pc}
  1e:   bf00        nop
  20:   9999999a    .word   0x9999999a
  24:   405ed999    .word   0x405ed999

00000028 <func2>:
  28:   eddf 7a02   vldr    s15, [pc, #8]   ; 34 <func2+0xc>
  2c:   ee20 0a27   vmul.f32    s0, s0, s15
  30:   4770        bx  lr
  32:   bf00        nop
  34:   42f6cccd    .word   0x42f6cccd
```

With -fsingle-precision-constant, both versions compile to the same as func2. Removing -fsingle-precision-constant and leaving -Wdouble-promotion generates the expected warning:

```
float.c: In function 'func1':
float.c:3:14: error: implicit conversion from 'float' to 'double' to match other operand of binary expression [-Werror=double-promotion]
     return a * 123.4;
              ^
```
There is another thing with mixing float and double: on targets with no FPU support whatsoever, the compiler will call software emulation lib for float, double and conversion wrappers. This makes the final executable code to grow.

On the other side -Wunsuffixed-float-constants can be really nasty with at least some versions of GCC, as there is no way to suffix a "double", but GCC nevertheless complains about the lack of suffix...
In order to write a usable/merge candidate patch, for -Wshadow, there are 3 "kinds" of shadowed variables:
1. `index` which is a very common issue with -Wshadow, as some some reason libc defined the `index` an `rindex` function.
2. `qstr` which is used as a type definition and local variables/function arguments
3. "regular" shadowed variables.

What's the micropython's way to resolve 1 & 2? index -> idx? , qstr -> ??
The `qstr` as a variable is something I've encountered before and had issues with.  I now try to use `qst` instead, ie `qstr qst;`.  See eg py/vm.c.

As for index ... why have you singled that out?  As far as I can tell, it's just a function, declared in string.h.
Ok for `qst`

About `index`: it is used as local variables / function arguments in several files (`binary.c`, `emitcommon.c`, ...), which include `<string.h>`
We can change `index` to `idx`.  But I will be sad when I merge that PR.
I wonder what to do about this ticket. On one hand, it says interesting, if not important, things. On the other hand, put in such broad scope and without (useful) patches, it sounds like "let's make life more complicated for maintainers". We already have too many warnings per my like for example, and that limits our choices. For example, -Werror precludes usage of #warning. Attempts to work that around bring more problems, like with new gcc versions it's possible to override -Werror for some warnings, but those options are not valid for older gcc versions and lead to errors (17598d49e1091e2745d8f01288f95007189cdcf5).

The same would happen with enabling other warnings - people who work with codebase regularly will just need to work them around. Productive approach to resolve this would be:
- Locally enable warnings one by one
- Review results, if there's just 1-2 real issues for dozens of false positives, just submit patches for them.
- Otherwise, focusedly argue for for enabling particular warning.
- Repeat.

That's a bit of work, true. But if there's no interest in doing that form contributors, it should be fair to turn that back and say there's no interest in doing that from core maintainers in doing that now and in foreseeable future. We surely care about quality assurance, that's why we have well-maintained testsuite. But beyond 3-4 useful warnings, the rest give 99% false positives, and dealing with them is not the best investment of effort.

Note that we do enable more warnings when it's grounded: 4e54c876a7236cbb50431f1f6d52c7be2052ed6f
Bottom line: should we keep this ticket as general RFC for reference, or close it with "specific patches welcome" resolution?
I would like to see the py/ core compile with as many warnings enabled as possible.  We can be more relaxed about specific ports, extmod (since it includes 3rd party code that likely fails many warnings), etc.  Making py/ core pass warnings only makes it more portable, and people can choose to enable them or not in their projects/ports.

Actually, I looked at -Wmissing-declarations and -Wmissing-prototypes the other day, and that lead to finding some real "errors", which were fixed in 969a6b37bfc655609e540053c2bdcce8a6fdc64d and 5318cc028aef9eb3edd88b01cd0e5b43c378fd83.

So I think we can go through the warnings and fix the ones that are easy to fix.  Then revisit what to do.
> I would like to see the py/ core compile with as many warnings enabled as possible.

Yeah, I'm sure too, the question who will do that (and why)?

> Actually, I looked at -Wmissing-declarations and -Wmissing-prototypes the other day

Cool. I wanted to run http://clang-analyzer.llvm.org/scan-build.html on uPy for ~3 months. Then I closed browser tab with that page, understanding I'm not getting to it anytime soon.

Anyway, just trying to triage old issues and close inactive ones. This ticket is active then.
> the question who will do that (and why)?

Me, because I want uPy to be as best it can be :)
uPy now compiles with more warnings enabled (the ones checked true in the first comment of this issue).  These warnings are enabled on unix/ port.

The rest of the warnings are not going to be fixed in the foreseeable future.
